awd_titl_txt: Conference: 2025 CISE Computer System Research PI Meeting
awd_abstract_narration:
The purpose of this project is to plan and organize the 2025 National Science Foundation (NSF) Principal Investigator (PI) Meeting of Computer System Research (CSR) Program, held in Boca Raton, FL Sept 17-18, 2025. The purpose of the meeting is to bring together active PIs and Program Directors (PDs) to exchange information and ideas to continue to advance research and explore new computer systems research directions. The program is planned for two days and will include keynotes, presentations by the PIs of featured projects, panel discussions, breakout meetings, poster sessions, an evening reception, and "office hours" with Program Directors.  Successful outcomes of this work will inform both PIs and NSF PDs.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This project supported the planning and organization of the 2025 National Science Foundation Computer Systems Research (CSR) Principal Investigator Meeting, held September 18–19, 2025, at Florida Atlantic University in Boca Raton, Florida. The meeting brought together 142 participants from the computer systems research community, including NSF-funded investigators, students, and NSF representatives. Its purpose was to share results from NSF-supported research, identify emerging research challenges, strengthen connections across the research community, and provide opportunities for researchers and NSF program staff to exchange perspectives on future directions.

The meeting provided a broad forum for communicating advances in computer systems research. The technical program included two keynote presentations, 57 short presentations by principal investigators, more than 117 research posters, six focused breakout sessions, panel discussions, NSF question-and-answer sessions and office hours, and opportunities for informal technical exchange. These activities exposed participants to research spanning computer hardware and software systems, artificial intelligence infrastructure, edge computing, energy-efficient computing, quantum computing, autonomous and cyber-physical systems, cybersecurity, and computing education.

An important intellectual outcome of the meeting was the identification and discussion of emerging research opportunities that cut across traditional areas of computer systems. Six breakout sessions examined AI systems for the next decade; energy-aware computing systems; edge AI and ultra-low-power computing; system support for quantum computing; autonomous and cyber-physical systems; and the future of computer systems research and education. Participants discussed challenges such as supporting increasingly large and distributed AI models, reducing the energy and resource demands of computing, bringing advanced AI capabilities to mobile and resource-constrained devices, making emerging quantum systems more usable, improving the safety and reliability of autonomous systems, and preparing students for a rapidly changing computing environment. These discussions provided both researchers and NSF program staff with community perspectives on research needs and promising future directions.

The project also produced broader impacts by strengthening the national computer systems research community. The meeting created opportunities for investigators from different institutions and technical areas to discover related work, exchange ideas, and identify potential collaborators. Poster sessions and networking activities enabled detailed conversations that complemented the formal presentations, while NSF panels and office hours gave researchers opportunities to interact directly with program staff.

Students and early-career researchers benefited from exposure to a wide range of current systems research and from opportunities to present their work, receive feedback, and develop professional connections. Florida Atlantic University students also participated in supporting the meeting, gaining experience with a national scientific event.

Overall, the project successfully created a national forum for disseminating NSF-supported research, encouraging collaboration, identifying emerging computer systems research challenges, and strengthening communication between the research community and NSF. The meeting helped researchers look beyond individual projects to consider shared technical challenges and future research opportunities that will influence the development of computing systems supporting artificial intelligence, autonomous technologies, emerging computing platforms, and other applications important to society.
